result:
No, this wording has real problems and shouldn't be published as-is. Three issues:

1. **"open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems"** — conflates the MIT license (a permission grant) with a safety/fitness claim. MIT explicitly disclaims all warranties ("AS IS," no fitness for purpose) — saying the license makes it "safe" contradicts the license text itself.

2. **"passed all our internal tests"** — fine as a fact, but as written it's doing rhetorical work to imply broader assurance than internal testing provides. Should be specific about what was tested, not left to imply "thoroughly vetted."

3. **"fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is the biggest risk. PCI DSS compliance isn't something a project can self-declare from internal testing; it's normally established via formal assessment (QSA audit, SAQ, etc.) against a specific implementation/environment. Claiming "fully compliant" here is an unsubstantiated regulated-use compliance claim, and payment software is exactly the area where that kind of claim creates real liability exposure. I'd flag this to legal directly rather than approve it — whether PayCheck can claim any PCI-related status isn't something to resolve in a README edit, it needs a qualified compliance/legal review.

Suggested rewrite for the non-compliance parts:

> "PayCheck is released under the MIT license, which permits use, modification, and distribution — including in commercial and production settings — subject to the license's 'as is' terms and disclaimer of warranty. It has passed our internal test suite [link/describe scope]. This project has not undergone independent PCI DSS assessment; teams handling cardholder data are responsible for their own compliance validation."

Bottom line for legal: pull the "safe for production" and "fully compliant with PCI" claims before publishing — the first misstates what MIT grants, the second is an unverified regulated-use claim.
